🐛 Bug
I noticed that when torch.save() is used on a narrowed version of a tensor, it saves the whole tensor (original tensor), but when using torch.load() it returns the narrowed tensor. To me, this looks like a bug because it saves something more than what it is intended, and we are not able to recover this redundant info. For that, I wrote a simple example, and you can check the output to see what I mean:
import torch
import os


x= torch.randint(0, 100, size=(10000,8), dtype=torch.long)

y1 = x.narrow(dim=0, start=0, length=10)
torch.save({"y": y1},"y1.pth")

y2 = x.narrow(dim=0, start=0, length=10).detach().clone()
torch.save({"y": y2},"y2.pth")


loaded_y1 = torch.load("y1.pth")["y"]
loaded_y2 = torch.load("y2.pth")["y"]

if torch.equal(loaded_y1, loaded_y2):
    print("loaded_y1==loaded_y2")

if torch.equal(loaded_y1, y1):
    print("loaded_y1==y1")

print("size y1.pth (in Bytes)=", os.stat("y1.pth").st_size)
print("size y2.pth (in Bytes)=", os.stat("y2.pth").st_size)

This is the output of the above script:

loaded_y1==loaded_y2
loaded_y1==y1
size y1.pth (in Bytes)= 640754
size y2.pth (in Bytes)= 1394

As you can see, both “y1.pth” and “y2.pth” are equal, but “y1.pth” is much larger because it saves the mother tensor, while we are not able to recover it.

The incorrect processing relates to 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/utils/bottleneck/__main__.py
    
    
         Line 119
      in
      b6f4bb0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def print_autograd_prof_summary(prof, mode, sortby='cpu_time', topk=15): 
        
    
  

.
For simplicity, here's a copy of the code
def print_autograd_prof_summary(prof, mode, sortby='cpu_time', topk=15):
    valid_sortby = ['cpu_time', 'cuda_time', 'cpu_time_total', 'cuda_time_total', 'count']
    if sortby not in valid_sortby:
        warn = ('WARNING: invalid sorting option for autograd profiler results: {}\n'
                'Expected `cpu_time`, `cpu_time_total`, or `count`. '
                'Defaulting to `cpu_time`.')
        print(warn.format(sortby))
        sortby = 'cpu_time'

    if mode == 'CUDA':
        cuda_warning = ('\n\tBecause the autograd profiler uses the CUDA event API,\n'
                        '\tthe CUDA time column reports approximately max(cuda_time, cpu_time).\n'
                        '\tPlease ignore this output if your code does not use CUDA.\n')
    else:
        cuda_warning = ''

    sorted_events = sorted(prof.function_events,
                           key=lambda x: getattr(x, sortby), reverse=True)
    topk_events = sorted_events[:topk]

    result = {
        'mode': mode,
        'description': 'top {} events sorted by {}'.format(topk, sortby),
        'output': torch.autograd.profiler.build_table(topk_events),
        'cuda_warning': cuda_warning
    }

    print(autograd_prof_summary.format(**result))

Here topk_events = sorted_events[:topk] followed by  'output': torch.autograd.profiler.build_table(topk_events) is incorrect. The table is built by using only the topk_events (instead of all events), and therefore all mentioned percentages and total times will be wrong in the resulting table.
By using the build_table function, one does not go through 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/autograd/profiler.py
    
    
         Line 36
      in
      9909327
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def populate_cpu_children(self): 
        
    
  


yielding different CPU times compared with 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/autograd/profiler.py
    
    
         Line 361
      in
      9909327
    
  
  
    

        
          
           def table(self, sort_by=None, row_limit=100, header=None, top_level_events_only=False): 
        
    
  


which does go through populate_cpu_children via _check_finish.
Finally, torch.utils.bottleneck sorts the table based on 
  
    
      pytorch/torch/utils/bottleneck/__main__.py
    
    
         Line 186
      in
      b6f4bb0
    
  
  
    

        
          
           autograd_prof_sortby = 'cpu_time_total' 
        
    
  


For the torch.autograd.profiler.profile profiler with use_cuda=True, sorting based on cuda_time_total might be more reliable (see #44784).

Additional context
See https://discuss.pytorch.org/t/confusion-about-torch-autograd-profiler-profile-api/87773 for an example related to this issue.

In https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/bottleneck.html it is highlighted that

Ops that do synchronize appear to be extremely expensive under regular CPU-mode profilers. In these case where timings are incorrect, the CUDA-mode autograd profiler may be helpful.

However, below experiments show that these CPU times might be unreliable altogether, even when used with torch.autograd.profiler.profile with use_cuda=True.
To reproduce

import copy
import torch
from torch import nn
from torch.utils._benchmark import Timer


parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument('--sync', action='store_true')

# Initialization
a = torch.randn(1024, 2, 256, device='cuda')
b = torch.randn(1024, 2, 256, device='cuda')

self_attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(256, 8).to('cuda')
layers = nn.ModuleList([copy.deepcopy(self_attention) for _ in range(10)])


def run_test(a, b, layers):
    for layer in layers:
        if args.sync:

        a = layer(a+b, a+b, a)[0]

timer = Timer(stmt='run_test(a, b, layers)', globals=globals())

🚀 Feature
Motivation
Current torch.all/torch.any and Tensor.all, Tensor.any only support bool/uint8. This is inconvenient when trying to write numpy-compatible code like
def somefunc(x):
    # x can be a numpy.ndarray or torch.Tensor instance
    if x.all():
        ....

It is also inconsistent with torch.logical_and et al., which work with all integer and float dtypes just fine.
Note that torch.all/any aren't documented as public API because they don't support all dtypes (see #7539 (comment)), that'd be nice to fix too.
Pitch

Add support for all dtypes to torch.any/all.
Document torch.all and torch.any as public API at https://pytorch.org/docs/master/torch.html#comparison-ops

Alternatives
The builtins all and any do work:
>>> t = torch.tensor([1, 2], dtype=torch.float64)                          
>>> all(t)                                                                 
True
>>> torch.all(t)                                                           
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<ipython-input-78-1c35bb87b542>", line 1, in <module>
    torch.all(t)
RuntimeError: all only supports torch.uint8 and torch.bool dtypes

however, they are orders of magnitude slower:
>>> t = torch.ones(10000, dtype=torch.bool)                                
>>> %timeit all(t)                                                         
10.9 ms ± 54.9 µs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100 loops each)

8.74 µs ± 57.1 ns per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 100000 loops each)

🐛 Bug
torch.equal(t1, t2) is slower than its alternative torch.eq(t1, t2).all() on GPU. The bug manifests itself after doing "some computation" (as for example self-attention). The only difference between both alternatives is that torch.equal(t1, t2) checks the sizes before proceeding and therefore works for all possible t1 and t2, while torch.eq(t1, t2).all() only works for non-empty t1 and t2 of the same size.
To Reproduce
import copy
import timeit
import torch
from torch import nn

# Before self-attention (some computation)
c = torch.randn(1024, 2, 256, device='cuda')
d = torch.randn(1024, 2, 256, device='cuda')

t1 = timeit.timeit('torch.eq(c, d).all()', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t2 = timeit.timeit('torch.eq(c, d).all()', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t3 = timeit.timeit('torch.eq(c, d).all()', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3

print(f"First time with eq/all (before self-attention): {t1: .4f} ms")
print(f"Second time with eq/all (before self-attention): {t2: .4f} ms")
print(f"Third time with eq/all (before self-attention): {t3: .4f} ms\n")

t1 = timeit.timeit('torch.equal(c, d)', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t2 = timeit.timeit('torch.equal(c, d)', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t3 = timeit.timeit('torch.equal(c, d)', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3

print(f"First time with equal (before self-attention): {t1: .4f} ms")
print(f"Second time with equal (before self-attention): {t2: .4f} ms")
print(f"Third time with equal (before self-attention): {t3: .4f} ms\n")

# Perform self-attention (some computation)
a = torch.randn(1024, 2, 256, device='cuda')
b = torch.randn(1024, 2, 256, device='cuda')

self_attention = nn.MultiheadAttention(256, 8).to('cuda')
layers = nn.ModuleList([copy.deepcopy(self_attention) for _ in range(20)])

for layer in layers:
    a = layer(a+b, a+b, a)[0]

# After self-attention (some computation)
t1 = timeit.timeit('torch.eq(c, d).all()', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t2 = timeit.timeit('torch.eq(c, d).all()', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t3 = timeit.timeit('torch.eq(c, d).all()', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3

print(f"Second time with eq/all (after self-attention): {t2: .4f} ms")
print(f"Third time with eq/all (after self-attention): {t3: .4f} ms\n")

t2 = timeit.timeit('torch.equal(c, d)', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3
t3 = timeit.timeit('torch.equal(c, d)', number=1, globals=globals())*1e3

print(f"Second time with equal (after self-attention): {t2: .4f} ms")
print(f"Third time with equal (after self-attention): {t3: .4f} ms\n")

After #43879 is landed PyTorch's floor_divide operator will be consistent with floor division in Python3 and NumPy. The new behavior is:
floor_divide(a, b) = torch.true_divide(a, b).floor_()

And the old behavior is:
floor_divide(a, b) = torch.true_divide(a, b).trunc_()

For example, -5 // 3 = -2 in Python3 and PyTorch after #43879, but -5 // 3 = -1 in C, C++, and PyTorch before #43879. The behavior is equivalent when the divisor and dividend are both positive or both negative, but different if one is positive and the other negative.
PyTorch's ONNX behavior still reflects the historic floor division behavior, however, and needs to be updated to be consistent.

Only attaching the proposal here, will add the colab from @bhosmer once I finish updating it.
Problem:

Consider _convolution implementation (runs before autograd, selects cpu/cuda implementation to do the actual work). Today, this is registered to both the CPU and Autograd keys via CatchAll mechanism, which means that we will use this implementation even if autograd is disabled (e.g., by NonVariableTypeMode). When we get rid of CatchAll, we still need to make sure these implementations get registered to CPU key. So for example, _convolution would have to be registered to CPU, CUDA, AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA. This is pretty wordy and a bit difficult for people to understand.

Solution: Offer synthetic dispatch keys which map to multiple dispatch keys, so that you can conveniently refer to “CPU, CUDA, AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA” all in one go. We call these alias dispatch keys.
Proposal:

Distinguish between runtime dispatch keys (keys that actually show up in the dispatch table) and alias dispatch keys (dispatch keys which map to other dispatch keys). Alias keys have precedence, but they are always lower precedence than runtime keys. New keys bolded.

Runtime keys: CPU, CUDA, XLA, AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA, AutogradXLA (previously PreAutogradXLA)
Alias keys: AutogradDispatchCPUOrCUDA > Math > Autograd (previously a runtime key, now alias)


When you register a kernel for an alias key, you register the kernel for some set of dispatch keys.

AutogradDispatchCPUOrCuda => CPU, CUDA, AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA
Autograd => AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA, AutogradXLA
Math => CPU, CUDA, XLA, AutogradCPU, AutogradCUDA, AutogradXLA (e.g., DefaultBackend and Autograd)


If a runtime dispatch key has multiple kernels, which kernel wins is done based on precedence of alias keys (but runtime keys always have precedence).

Example: convolution. Kernels are registered to AutogradDispatchCPUOrCuda (at::native::_convolution), Autograd (derivatives.yaml), XLA (XLA implementation)

AutogradXLA => derivatives.yaml (only key that maps to this key)
AutogradCPU => at::native::_convolution (beats derivatives.yaml because AutogradDispatchCPUOrCuda > Autograd)




Then there’s some mumbling you have to do about Math versus backend key: when there’s a direct registration to backend key X, AutogradX key should skip picking up Math kernel.

[Update]: Additional key DefaultBackend:
What are the use cases?
Consider operator at::sign which currently

has no dispatch section in native_functions.yaml => Use TypeDefault and registered as CatchAll

note this kernel works for all backends as it just redirect calls to at::sign_out which has a dispatch section in native_functions.yaml.
at::sign_out actually doesn’t have derivative defined.


It has an entry in derivatives.yaml.

The problem happens when we try to move at::sign from catchAll to Math key, since Math > Autograd, Math kernel would just override the Autograd kernel which was expected to be used. (Autograd > catchAll)
Proposed solution?
This requires us to have a way in native_functions.yaml to say

hey please only use TypeDefault::sign for inference, and use kernel from Autograd for training if available

solution: DefaultBackend > Math > Autograd
for every op that has an entry in derivatives.yaml but no explicit dispatch section in native_functions.yaml, register TypeDefault::op to DefaultBackend. VariableType::op to Autograd.
What does it mean to current native_functions.yaml?
Ops like at::sign is currently registered to catchAll, they should be registered as DefaultBackend (by adding DefaultBackend in native_functions.yaml) before we can move catchAll kernels to Math.
Ops we need to move has the following properties:

it doesn’t have dispatch section in native_functions.yaml
its kernel works for all backends (calling ops using at::) .
its implementation uses an op doesn’t have autograd. (like _out function)
it either has an entry in derivatives.yaml (or it’s inplace version of the op), or has a manual Autograd kernel.

In general this improves native_functions.yaml that:
by look at native_functions.yaml,


we know exactly which backend the kernel support (it was not accurate due to dispatchStub and is_sparse() etc),


where does the training support for this op should come from for each backend.

The profiler is a useful tool to gain insight regarding the operations run inside a model, and is a commonly used tool to diagnose performance issues and optimize models. This RFC seeks to describe how the profiler will be integrated with torch.distributed.
Example use cases
Python:
# directly calling c10d APIs from python
with torch.autograd.profiler.profile() as prof:
    pending_work = []
    for i in range(5):
        w = dist.all_reduce(torch.ones(i), async_op=True)
        pending_work.append(ww)
    for w in pending_work:
        w.wait()
            
# Should show time and ideally shapes for each input
print(prof.key_averages.table())
C++:
// directly calling c10d APIs from C++ 
{
    torch::autograd::profiler::enableProfiler();
    std::vector<Work> w;
    for (i = 0 ; i < 10; ++i) { 
      auto work = process_group->allreduce(torch::ones(i));
      w.push_back(work);
    } 
    for (const auto& w : work) {
      w.wait();
    }
    torch::autograd::profiler::disableProfiler();
    // We should expect that the events contain the entire asynchronous running 
    // time, not just the synchronous part of the call into allreduce().

}
DDP example:
# DDP training, should include profiling of c10d calls. 
ddp_model = DDP(model, device_ids=[torch.cuda.current_device()])
# forward pass of models with c10d collectives should be profiled. 
with torch.autograd.profiler.profile() as prof:
    outputs = ddp_model(torch.randn(20, 10).to(torch.cuda.current_device()))
    loss_fn(outputs, labels).backward()
Note that above, we can probably get information about the shape of tensors that were allreduced as well, which can be input into the RECORD_FUNCTION macro. This can potentially provide better debugging information in the case of mismatches, as the profiler shapes for each call would differ across ranks, giving clues into the source of the mismatch.
Current state of distributed profiling
Profiling within the RPC framework has been enabled (#39675). Currently, profiling a DDP model outputs the expected information about native torch operators ran in the model's forward and backwards passes, but no information about allreduce (or any other collective calls that the user might have in their model definition):

r of Calls

---------

aten::normal_                        0.10%            180.898us        0.10%            180.898us        90.449us         0.09%            181.057us        90.528us         2

The following use of the record_function context manager doesn't work for our use cases either:
with profiler():
    with record_funcion("allreduce"):
        work = dist.all_reduce(async_op = True)
    work.wait()
since the async portion of the allreduce would not be profiled (similar to the issue encountered with RPC profiling).
Design and Implementation
We will follow an approach similar to the way async functions in torch.distributed.rpc are profiled, and an example of this approach being generalized to general distributed functions is in #44436. At a high level, we would like insert RecordFunction objects that will run profiling callbacks at the beginning and end of the functions that we'd like to profile.
To make this work for async functions, we have to extend the lifetime of the RecordFunction so that the profiler's end callbacks do not run when the sync part of the function exits (which is what it'd do by default).
In order to do this, we have introduced an API called rf._call_end_callbacks_on_future which schedules the RecordFunction's end callbacks to be run after the future is marked as completed. This returns a new future that can be waited on, after which we have a guarantee that the future has been profiled.
In order to support this, we would need to provide a get_future() API that converts Work to Future for both NCCL work and Gloo. #42335 adds get_future() for NCCL and #44436 adds it for Gloo. Given this, we could profile collectives from python via:
# This will be wrapped into a function so users don't have to call with record_function(....)
with record_function as rf:
    work = dist.all_reduce(....)
    rf._call_end_callbacks_on_future(work.get_future()
# Work can now be awaited within the profiler scope outside of record_function, and will have
# its correct execution time recorded.
Note: the above is probably a short/medium-term solution, and in the long term we'd probably want to merge Work and Future so that we have only a single representation of asynchronous work object in distributed code.
At the C++ level, the profiling would look something like the following:
auto handle = record_function_enter(...)
auto work = process_group->allreduce(....)
profiler::_call_end_callbacks_on_future(handle, work.getFuture())
Note that this is quite similar to how we profile rpc_async calls from JIT functions, which is entirely in C++: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/master/torch/csrc/distributed/rpc/torchscript_functions.cpp#L77
One thing to keep in mind as @pritamdamania87 mentioned is that since the ProcessGroup.hpp interface should be stable due to c10d extension API, we will have to add this profiling to collective ops individually in ProcessGroupGloo and ProcessGroupNCCL.
Combining profiles across nodes
As mentioned by #43231, it would be good to have an API such as torch.distributed.profiling.combine_profiles which allows any rank to collect profiles from different ranks. This can be implemented by using the recently introduced torch.distributed.gather_object() APIs (#42189), we would just need to ensure that class profile can be pickled.  We can then combine profiles locally and export a single trace for all nodes using prof.export_chrome_trace().

🚀 Feature
Support for complex-valued torch.cholesky.
Motivation
Pytorch 1.6 supports complex-valued tensors, however, most of the matrix operations cannot be written in terms of their real analogue  (in contrast to e.g. multiplication, which currently also does not support complex-valued data). Cholesky decomposition is important in decorrelating e.g. Monte Carlo data. The MAGMA backend also supports Cholesky decompositions for complex-valued data.
Pitch
torch.cholesky supports complex-valued data.

    if depth>0:

    x = bar(depth)
    logging.info('grad enabled: {}'.format(torch.is_grad_enabled()))
    return x

    assert not torch.is_grad_enabled()
    y = foo(0)

🐛 Bug
The newly introduced join() API does not work with model.no_sync() since the latter disables synchronization in the bwd pass (allreduce, unused params allreduce, bucket rebuilting allreduce, etc) while the join() API currently expects synchronization every backwards pass. An example of the issue:
Rank 0 is joined:

It schedules the "shadow" allreduce to detect presence of non-joined ranks
It schedules an allreduce to sync module buffers in the forward pass
It schedules allreduces for the backwards pass

Rank 1 is not joined, but no_sync=True

It schedules the "shadow" allreduce as above
It schedules the allreduce to sync modules buffers in the forward pass
It skips the allreduce in the backward pass and thus goes back to 1, thus causing a mismatch of collective operations.

To fix this, we can schedule an allreduce where then non-joined ranks communicate whether they are running under the no_sync manager or not. Joined processes will contribute a 0 to this allreduce.
If the result is nonzero (ideally we should assert it's equal to the effective world size if the result is not zero), then the joined process will skip its allreduces it would have scheduled to simulate the backwards pass communication. It would also need to set its local self.require_forward_param_sync = False in this case, since no_sync() skips the forward pass module buffer synchronization in the next iteration.

🚀 Feature
I want to be able to determine the version of libtorch in my c++ binary in cases where I don't have access to the python library.
Something like:
#define TORCH_VERSION_MAJOR=1
#define TORCH_VERSION_MINOR=6
#define TORCH_VERSION_PATCH=0

Motivation
This is useful for

Turning off torch features depending on the version of torch we are running
Debugging which version of torch is installed in production where different versions may be running.

Pitch

I'm a developer trying to upgrade the API, but a backwards incompatible API change requires me to refactor code before upgrading.  I need to roll this out so I want to only enable the new features if I build my application for the new version of torch.
I'm a site reliability engineer and I am rolling out a the server deploy with a new version of libtorch.  There is a bug that is claimed to be fixed in the newer version of torch and I want to verify that the new version was deployed when I validate this issue is resolved.

Alternatives
Currently I am pulling the version from the strings in libtorch_cpu.so, but this didn't get updated in v1.6.0.  This is an unreliable hack solution that I would like to remove.
strings libtorch_cpu.so | egrep -A1 pytorch_version
pytorch_version
1.5.0

pytorch has the version number baked into the pip install and in the torch.version.  For my purposes I don't have access to either of these as we are not using python in our production environment and the shared libraries are built separate from the ones in the pip wheel.
Additional context
I recently upgraded to libtorch version 1.6.0 to resolve a segfault on destruction of DeviceThreadHandlePool which seemed related to: #36416.  After upgrading I am still seeing some segfaults on destruction, but was worried that I might not have deployed the new version of libtorch.   By looking at other strings in that library I believe I am at v1.6.0, but I wasted some time on the red herring of the 1.5.0 version in the strings of libtorch_cpu.so and would like to avoid that in the future.
